title: Crosby delivery: Owning work enables workflow redesign
desc: Links faster contracting to client context, lawyer feedback and non-hourly incentives, with humans directing and verifying agents.

kps.k: Crosby advances a service-delivery thesis: owning legal work, not just supplying software, enables AI-led workflow redesign.
kps.d: Daniels and Sarihan describe a contract-focused law firm that receives agreements, edits terms and handles negotiation. Nicole Seah’s profile adds that Crosby employs lawyers and assumes liability. The founders argue that direct delivery exposes client preferences and working practices that software vendors may miss; the Sequoia host frames this as an operational-feedback advantage. This positions Crosby as a provider of legal outcomes rather than a tool that clients must deploy themselves, but does not establish that owning a firm is necessary for successful automation.

qs.q: The only way that we could automate this properly was to build our own law firm.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: They employ lawyers, own liability, and take on the work end to end.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The commercial model rewards faster negotiation rather than more recorded hours.
kps.d: Sarihan defines Crosby’s guiding metric as its cumulative review time across negotiation rounds—not the full elapsed time to signature—and seeks fewer exchanges as well as faster handling. In Change Order, Daniels describes per-contract purchasing as a flexible alternative to expanding internal staffing. Elsewhere, he says Crosby accepted the risk of negative daily margins to motivate productivity improvements. He links responsive counsel to quarterly revenue timing, citing unspecified surveys and qualifying the effect as deals slipping rather than usually disappearing. These accounts explain the intended incentives, not demonstrated profitability or causal revenue gains.

qs.q: If you add up all the time that Crosby has spent looking at a contract, that’s our north star metric.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: For us, it's really thinking about like how do we minimize those back and forths and also get faster every time.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Reported speed gains support a promising but narrowly evidenced human-plus-AI model.
kps.d: Daniels reports one-to-two-hour maximum turnaround in Change Order; the Sequoia transcript reports median reviews slightly below an hour. Neither account supplies a detailed comparative study. Seah’s two-week reporting visit provides a concrete observation: a lawyer completed a known NDA in four minutes and 53 seconds, against an approximately 58-minute unaided estimate supplied by a team member. She labels the improvement roughly tenfold but limits it to one sample and contract type. Her observation includes human review and correction, not autonomous delivery. Daniels also says AI trails humans on commercial-agreement benchmarks without identifying those benchmarks. Generalisable speed, quality and safety therefore remain unestablished.

qs.q: Sometimes their lawyer and we get it back to you in an hour or two max.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And structuring ourselves with lawyers in the loop in a really clever way allows us to have the oversight of lawyers and kind of all the safety and the quality that I mentioned before, but see how much we can really push the limits on right now we do a contract review and median times are at a little under an hour.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Client context and lawyer feedback underpin the proposed technical advantage, but their durability remains contested.
kps.d: Daniels prioritises capturing counterparties, deal importance, prior concessions and internal knowledge through CRM and knowledge-tool integrations; access to Slack sales context remains an ambition. He treats timely use of this information as a potential durable advantage. The Sequoia discussion records a methodological tension: Sarihan requested evaluations while Daniels favoured immediate expert assessment and prompting feedback. That supports lawyer-led iteration, not dispensing with formal evaluation or verification before reliance. Seah raises competitive counterweights, including foundation models and incumbent firms’ internal technology investment.

qs.q: For contract negotiation, it sounds simple,  it's a legal negotiation, but we have to plug into a CRM and know who are the counter parties, what is the priority of this deal, what are the things that we have given on in the past for deals like this.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (legal services in the age of AI) · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: You know, John was constantly asking for evals, and I was like, “That’s fine, we’ll work on this, but I can look at it in 10 seconds and tell you, right?
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: The proposed lawyer role combines verification, agent direction and client judgment rather than residual proofreading.
kps.d: Crosby’s current account retains bar-admitted US lawyers and human judgment. Seah reports that the team deliberately designs for lawyer control and hopes automation will free time for difficult legal questions and client relationships. Daniels predicts that explaining expertise and prompting will become more valuable than repetition-based apprenticeship alone. These are design priorities and professional forecasts, not demonstrated improvements in training, working hours or trust. Seah identifies a continuing organisational tension between legal risk aversion and startup speed.

qs.q: We have like a human judgment, but um we have a lot of AI workflows we've built in to make that incredibly fast no matter what time of day.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: The team at Crosby is pretty opinionated that product choices really matter in preserving lawyer choice and agency.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Agent-led negotiation remains a future design vision, not evidence of autonomous commercial counsel.
kps.d: The founders envision agents encoding each party’s preferences, simulating collaborative negotiations and producing an auditable record as a starting point for agreement. Sarihan proposes separate data access and controlled communications, drawing an analogy to information walls. Seah describes a related ambition for personalised agents that encode lawyers’ expertise and negotiation styles. The supplied material does not demonstrate deployment, effective confidentiality safeguards or autonomous handling of complex agreements; present lawyer-supervised delivery must remain distinct from this broader automation thesis.

qs.q: **Ryan Daniel:** I think this is the most beautiful essence of what we hope we can achieve here, is being able to capture each party’s preferences with their own sets of agents, and have them simulate the negotiation and be able to show an auditable record of here was the first back and forth and then the fifth and the seventh and here’s where we netted.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: Lawyers that can create scalable agent versions of themselves which encode their expertise, client preferences, and negotiation style into parallelizable legal agents.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Capacity expansion could mean avoided hiring or newly served legal need, but neither establishes broad job displacement or access-to-justice gains.
kps.d: Daniels says customers retain legal headcount while clearing backlogs and improving stakeholder satisfaction, without supplying measurements. His anecdote that a two-lawyer client would otherwise need 20 lawyers is a qualified customer counterfactual, not evidence of 18 layoffs. Separately, he hopes much greater lawyer capacity could provide review where none currently occurs; the two-versus-500-contracts-per-hour comparison is hypothetical. This broader access aspiration differs from enterprise cost flexibility and lacks a concrete civil-legal-service programme or expansion timetable. Seah’s caution about long-term forecasts qualifies the founders’ explicitly optimistic five-to-ten-year outlook.

qs.q: And one of their lawyers said without Crosby, we'd be 20 lawyers today, which like the ratio is um I mean I think sorry, they're like over 80 sales people now.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And my hope is that if you can add so much leverage to lawyers that, like, rather than looking at two contracts an hour, they can look at 500, like, shouldn’t we be able to have more and more people getting serviced?
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This curated AI-native legal-provider voice supports the synthesis’s principal proposition that directly delivering legal work enables Crosby to redesign contracting workflows around AI, client context, rapid lawyer feedback and incentives other than maximising billable hours. Across the records, the recurring rationale is that operating the law firm gives Crosby control of the end-to-end workflow and access to the preferences, inputs and practitioner judgments needed to improve it. The sources also consistently describe the present model as human-plus-AI: lawyers retain judgment and oversight because AI alone is said to remain below human performance on commercial agreements. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis. Some accounts foreground service ownership and operational telemetry; others stress per-contract economics, margin pressure and company-specific integrations; and the Sequoia discussion extends the model toward agent-led negotiation and wider access. Those latter outcomes remain aspirations rather than demonstrated capabilities. Likewise, reported turnaround times, customer benefits and productivity gains are predominantly company self-reports, anecdotes or narrow observations, so support for the delivery thesis is stronger than evidence for its generalisable performance, durable competitive advantage or access-to-justice effects. These selected Crosby-associated sources should not be treated as representative of AI-native legal providers generally.

qs.q: The only way that we could automate this properly was to build our own law firm.

qs.q: And structuring ourselves with lawyers in the loop in a really clever way allows us to have the oversight of lawyers and kind of all the safety and the quality that I mentioned before, but see how much we can really push the limits on right now we do a contract review and median times are at a little under an hour.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This curated market/press voice supports the proposition that owning and delivering legal work enables AI-led workflow redesign while keeping lawyers responsible for judgment and verification. Seah’s profile presents Crosby as a legal-services provider that employs lawyers, assumes liability and handles matters end to end, rather than as a software vendor. It also aligns with the human-directed model: AI accelerates redlining, but lawyers review and alter its suggestions, while product design seeks to preserve lawyer agency and client relationships. Material variation lies in evidentiary confidence, not overall direction. The observed speed gain is confined to a known NDA and an internally supplied unaided comparison, so it does not establish general performance, quality or trust. Personalised agents and end-to-end agentic counsel are treated as ambitions, while foundation-model competition, incumbent investment and tension between legal risk aversion and startup speed remain unresolved. As this facet contains one curated profile, it should not be read as representative of market analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

elens.an: The two curated 2025 sources consistently accept the proposition that Crosby’s direct delivery of legal work—rather than sale of legal software alone—enables workflow redesign around AI. Their common reasoning is that operating the contract-focused law firm provides access to real workflows, client-specific risk preferences and rapid lawyer feedback, while aligning performance with contract turnaround rather than recorded hours. Both also describe a copilot model in current practice: lawyers retain oversight and judgment while AI workflows accelerate review. Material variation lies mainly in emphasis. Daniels’s Change Order interview stresses end-to-end service delivery, per-contract purchasing and the limits of AI relative to humans on commercial agreements. The Sequoia transcript places greater weight on telemetry, feedback loops and total turnaround time, and extends into agent-led negotiation and capacity expansion; however, those latter elements are presented as future aspirations rather than demonstrated adoption at scale. Across both sources, evidence for speed and customer effects remains predominantly company self-report, anecdote and unspecified benchmarking, so they support the operating thesis more strongly than they establish generalisable quality, safety or scale.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that Crosby’s ownership of end-to-end legal delivery enables workflow redesign around AI, client context and faster contracting rather than software deployment alone. Common supporting reasons are that Crosby employs lawyers, assumes liability and performs the work; direct delivery generates operational feedback and access to company-specific negotiating context; and commercial incentives focus attention on cumulative turnaround, fewer negotiation rounds and productivity rather than maximising billable hours. They also consistently describe a human-directed model in which lawyers retain judgment, control and client relationships. Material variation concerns evidentiary strength and future scope: founder accounts present telemetry, context integration, capacity expansion and agent orchestration largely as company claims or ambitions, while Seah contributes an observed speed demonstration but explicitly confines it to a known NDA sample and one contract type. Seah also stresses unresolved trust, organisational tension and competitive threats. Thus, the sources support the operating thesis without establishing generalisable quality or safety gains, the durability of Crosby’s advantage, autonomous agent-led negotiation, or broad access-to-justice effects.
